content: The term inner child is a concept in popular psychology that refers to the childlike aspect of an individual's psyche, often viewed as an independent entity within the mind. This concept is frequently used to explore subjective childhood experiences and the lingering effects of those experiences on a person’s emotional and psychological state. The inner child encompasses all emotional memories and experiences stored in the brain from the earliest stages of life. In the context of recovery programs, particularly the Twelve-Step Program, healing the inner child is considered a critical stage in overcoming addiction, abuse, trauma, or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The concept of the inner child gained prominence in the 1970s alongside the clinical understanding of codependency, which was initially referred to as Adult Children of Alcoholics Syndrome. Carl Jung referred to a similar concept as the Divine Child, while Emmet Fox called it the Wonder Child. Charles Whitfield named it the Child Within, and some psychotherapists describe it as the True Self. In Transactional Analysis, it is simply referred to as the Child. W. Missildine is believed to have been the first to use the term inner child in his 1963 book Your Inner Child of the Past. The idea of the wounded inner child is a variation of this concept, popularized by John Bradshaw, an American educator and a prominent figure in the self-help and pop psychology movements. Other notable contributors who have expanded on the inner child concept and its therapeutic applications include Lucia Capacchione, Louise Hay, Dr. Margaret Paul, and Pia Mellody.
